Photograph: Vadim Ghirdă/AP Opinion Rivers Europe’s rivers are running dry, and the knock-on effects are disastrous Yiannis Baboulias Droughts that were once a century now happen every year, and the impact on wildlife, industrial output and culture itself is catastrophic Wed 5 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share L ast week, 186 passengers had to be evacuated from the cruise ship Viking Ullur, after it ran aground on a sandbank in the Danube. Others have been left stranded , unable to move between Vienna and Budapest. Passengers stood on deck, the Habsburg splendour around them out of reach as the river fell to 41cm in Budapest, within 8cm of its 2018 all-time low. Elsewhere on the Hungarian stretch of the river, new record lows were recorded. Farther east in Romania , the Danube recorded its lowest water levels since 1996. A river’s flow is measured in cubic metres per second, and at Baziaș, where the river enters the country, it stood at 1,700m³/s, against a July average of 4,700m³/s. Ferry services were suspended, as were grain barges. While providing the most glamorous images, the Danube is just one of the major rivers veining through Europe that has been suffering through this summer’s drought. Farther north, the Rhine, perhaps the most vital fresh-water transport route in the continent, broke its own records, with levels at Kaub dropping to about 40cm, the level at which shipping runs in emergency mode, with barges loading as little as a fifth of normal capacity. The extent and frequency of these summer droughts has surprised even the most pessimistic expert observers. In 2018, Germany’s weather service designated that year a Jahrhundertsommer – a once-in-a-century summer – as the Rhine spent 132 days at low water. “The events of 2018 can’t be allowed to be repeated,” said Andreas Scheuer, then the federal transport minister. But they were. In 2022, EU scientists described the drought gripping the continent as the worst in at least 500 years . Then in 2025, Germany logged its driest March on record and another low-water summer. And this July, the Danube’s water level was at a low it didn’t reach until October during the 2018 drought. The crisis is now happening every year, and it’s arriving earlier. A study led by Dr Sehrish Usman at the University of Mannheim, working with European Central Bank economists, found that last summer’s heatwaves, droughts and floods hit a quarter of all EU regions, causing short-term losses of at least €43bn, with the total expected to reach €126bn by 2029. On the Rhine alone, the Kiel Institute has shown that a single month of low water cuts German industrial production by about 1%. The immense wildfires we’re seeing across the continent are not separate from this phenomenon, as the same mechanism is driving both: a hotter atmosphere is soaking up soil moisture faster than the rain can replenish it. That dry soil can’t feed the rivers, or the plants, which end up feeding the fires instead. France has recorded more than three times its annual average number of wildfires already this summer, as soil moisture is the lowest Météo-France has ever recorded this early in the season. The fires, like the river crisis, are arriving ahead of schedule. The damage these events inflict on the natural world is harder to put into numbers. In 2018, Swiss authorities pulled about a tonne of dead grayling from the Rhine (about 30% of the annual catch), as water temperatures surpassed 25C. By 2022, the reintroduced Atlantic salmon the river had spent decades nursing back could no longer reach their spawning grounds. Pollutant concentrations rise as water levels fall. On the Danube that year, oxygen levels fell close to the threshold below which trout can’t survive. Dredging was banned, and wastewater plants were placed on standby. Then this month, water levels dropped to the point where Romania was forced to shut down nuclear plants beside the Danube for the first time, as the reactors use river water to cool their cores, and if the river drops too far they can’t run safely. The country declared a nationwide state of emergency and detonated 180kg of explosives on the Bala canal to clear a rock obstructing the flow, buying the remaining reactor a few more days. Meanwhile in Hungary, the Paks nuclear plant, which normally supplies almost half of the country’s electricity, could be fully shut down within days. View image in fullscreen Underwater explosives are used to clear rocks and improve water flow to the Cernavoda nuclear power plant in Izvoarele, Romania, 3 August. Photograph: Andreea Alexandru/AP About seven years ago, when I first started looking into what’s happening to Europe’s great waterways, I contacted Christina Gruber , a marine biologist and artist based in Vienna, who has been watching this longer than most. I wanted to understand the effects these events have on the societies that have built big parts of their identity and culture around these rivers. She told me about an island her friends used to swim out to in the summer, to get away from the grownups. By 2019, people could walk to it. We’re also seeing the slow disappearance of the Danube’s fishers, all but gone from a river that has fed them since at least 300BC. The people who knew the river best were gone, as the water went with them. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion In 1986, the Italian polymath Claudio Magris travelled the Danube from source to delta and wrote a book about what a river means. The Danube was the connecting tissue of Mitteleuropa. Vienna’s concert halls, Budapest’s parliament, the Ottoman and Habsburg and Byzantine sediment accumulated along its banks over centuries, into much that we understand as a shared civilisation. The Rhine is Germany’s industrial spine, the artery that carried the coal and iron ore on which a particular idea of the country was built. Magris was already writing about a river in cultural decline before the water levels started being a central part of the question. “Century event” has disappeared from the official vocabulary, as seven consecutive years of records made it ridiculous, and replaced by superlatives such as “all-time low”, “historic”, “30-year low”. The problem is that this language still treats each summer as an exceptional incident, with hope for a recovery attached. But this assumption too, that Europe’s great rivers will keep being what they were, regardless of what we do to the climate that feeds them, should also be abandoned. Yiannis Baboulias is a Greek writer based in London. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Among those killed in the strike on Ansar included three children and two women, state media reports By Samantha Granville Published 15 August 2026, 12:24 BST Updated Just now Nine people have been killed in Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon, authorities say, in one of the deadliest days of attacks since an agreement aimed at reducing hostilities was announced in June. Lebanon's prime minister said seven people were killed in a strike on a house on the outskirts of Ansar in the Nabatieh district, which state media reported included three children and two women. Later on Saturday, another round of strikes hit the town of Deir al-Zahrani, killing two and injuring nine others, according to the Lebanese Ministry of Health. Israel's military said it had struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure" in response to what it described as an earlier action against its soldiers. Authorities say the strike in Ansar at around 04:30 (01:30 GMT) occurred where displaced families were living. Footage on social media shows large plumes of smoke permeating through the streets of the village as sirens ring out. Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned the attacks, saying the seven civilians killed were not "military infrastructure". "Israel must halt this escalation," he said. "For the security of our people and their right to life on their land are not subject to negotiation or bargaining." The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the incident that had prompted its strike on Ansar took place in the Ali al-Taher Ridge, a strategic high ground overlooking much of south-eastern Lebanon and of the war's most fiercely contested positions. Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) also reported a series of strikes around the ridge. Near the border, several homes were reportedly destroyed in Bint Jbeil, while Israeli forces opened heavy machine gun fire towards houses, according to NNA. Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - the armed group affiliated with Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory. The June ceasefire framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun condemned the Israeli strikes that had killed an entire family in Ansar and its "repeated violations" of the framework, which he said sent a "clear message" to the US-led negotiations. Hezbollah was not involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations. The IDF says it will continue to remove threats to Israeli citizens and soldiers operating in the security zone - the 10km-deep military buffer in southern Lebanon occupied by Israel. Despite a reduction in fighting following the June agreements, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued. On Friday, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem criticised the Lebanese authorities over the implementation of the framework, accusing them of putting pressure on the Lebanese army while Israeli attacks continued. "How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" he said. Lebanese and Israeli negotiators are set to meet for an eighth round of negotiations in September, but a final date has not been set. https://www.kyivpost.com/post/83259.text: War Ukraine World North America Latin America Europe Eastern Europe Middle East Africa Asia Economy Business Technology Finance Energy Agriculture Videos Podcasts Analysis Corruption Watch Opinions Culture Reviews History Sports Classifieds Spotlight Cartoons EN UK War in Ukraine Culture Russia How Russia’s Cultural Projects Conceal Their Human Atrocities In brief: Russia continues to use culture and internationally recognized artists to advance its influence abroad and promote the normalization of relations with Moscow despite the ongoing war. Russian violinists Vadim Repin and Mikhail Simonyan are examples of Kremlin-linked cultural engagement that, ultimately, cannot be separated from Russia’s actions in Ukraine. by David Root | Aug. 30, 2026, 4:24 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Russian violonist Vadim Repin performs during the 17th Victoires de la Musique Classique ceremony (France’s classical music award) on Feb. 8, 2010 in Montpellier, southern France. AFP PHOTO / PASCAL GUYOT (Photo by PASCAL GUYOT / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip In early November a musical concert of appalling hypocrisy will occur in Annapolis, Maryland. Russian violinist Vadim Repin , who is aligned with Vladimir Putin, will perform at the Annapolis Symphony Orchestra (ASO). Unfortunately, most Americans are oblivious to Russia’s weaponized culture. Russia exports musicians to the international stage to divert attention away from their war crimes. This so-called “soft culture weapon” increasingly bolsters Russia’s war. Serenading audiences with Russian artists induces viewers to embrace Russian culture on a personal level. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Meanwhile, another Russian violin controversy is brewing. In July, U.S. Commissioner of Fine Arts Rodney Mims Cook, Jr. requested Mikhail Simonyan to entertain artists, celebrities, and diplomats in Atlanta. A Facebook post, “Russian embassy in USA,” called it a friendly reset for “Russian American cultural ties to restore normal relations.” Advertisement Simonyan’s Pro Putin stance and his previous position at the Novosibirsk Military Commissariat makes him an unlikely peace facilitator. He previously entertained Russian troops wearing “Z” patches , a rallying symbol of Russian fascism. Cook, an artist administrator turned foreign affairs expert, recently negotiated secretly with Kremlin officials at the St. Petersburg Economic forum. He discussed initiating a ceasefire predicated on a Russian orchestra performance. These negotiations with Putin aristocrats represent the height of political obfuscation making America a laughing stock of foreign affairs. Other Topics of Interest Moscow Sentences Ex-Ukrainian Adviser Arestovych to 11 Years in Prison A Moscow military court has sentenced former Ukrainian adviser Oleksiy Arestovych in absentia to 11 years in prison for “false information.” Not surprisingly, Vadim Repin’s performance has met outcry by the American Ukrainian community. They understand how Russian cultural propaganda fuels the Kremlin’s authoritative power and influence. Ukraine’s US embassy has also urged rejection of Repin’s performance. Repin also known as “Putin’s violinist” presents himself as apolitical but is financially and ideologically connected to Putin. This differs from the fascist Simonyan, who should have been banned from entering America. Advertisement In April 2022, Putin ceremoniously declared Repin to be “People’s artist of Russia.” Rather eerily this occurred as the press unveiled the Bucha massacre whereby Russian forces murdered 400 hundred Ukrainian civilians. Likewise, Simonyan has also been praised by Putin. Following the Kremlin money trail reveals a unique form of bribery. Repin’s arts festival regularly receives grants from Putin’s fund for cultural initiatives . Critics claim the foundation supports projects aligned with Russia’s war. The Putin violinist recently applied for another $1.2 million grant. To repay the favor Repin stays silent about Russia’s war. Repin’s wife, Svetlana Zakharova is a sanctioned member of the United Russia party. She is a renowned ballerina and former Kremlin politician who openly promotes Kremlin authoritarianism. Palm Beach Florida removed Repin from a performance scheduled for March 2026. The International Organization Arts against Aggression claimed the concert timely coincided with a meeting between Russian and American envoys to bolster bilateral trade and economic cooperation. Repin’s manager admitted the concert was a “bridge building effort.” More evidence that Russia uses its artists to propel Kremlin influence. Advertisement Repin’s performance has been shuttered in numerous European countries. When Repin was rejected in Hungary , Ukraine’s foreign minister stated that “Russia’s culture is a culture of genocide and war crimes that has no place on any International stage.” Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs laments the cancellation of Russian artists as “xenophobic.” This reinforces how Russia’s state sponsored cultural performances are a coverup for Russia’s atrocities. They fail to mention that Russia’s Orthodox Church , a pillar of Russia’s culture, endorses the annihilation of 40 million Ukrainian civilians – making Russia the real xenophobic culprit. In order to augment its global influence, Russia uses musicians and artists to portray a good Russia image aimed at laundering their human atrocities. This increases the chances of sanction removal and forgiveness for their alleged 213,000 war crimes . Unfortunately, it’s a ploy aimed at rebuilding their war economy in preparation for future wars. This same pattern of forgiveness, then aggression, occurred after Putin directed the invasion of Georgia (2008), Syria (2015), and Ukraine (2014). Advertisement The partially taxpayer funded ASO refuses to cancel Repin’s performance despite Russia’s escalating atrocities. Since the beginning of 2026, the UN reported 12,477 Ukrainian civilians killed or injured, which is more than double the same period in 2024. Another 1.6 million Ukrainian children are held as prisoners behind an iron curtain in Russian occupied Ukraine. Former Annapolis Orchestra Director Edgar Herrera cancelled Repin immediately after Russia’s 2022 full scale invasion of Ukraine. Rescheduling him now under the guise of friendly Russian relations while Russia increases its terror is a moral travesty. Now is the time for America to stand in solidarity with Ukraine and ban Pro-Kremlin artists supporting Russian’s genocide. https://hungarytoday.hu/deafening-silenc.text: Deafening Silence as Government Shuts Down Conservative News Website “The Mandiner website is now inaccessible, and it will remain that way forever,” Konfront wrote on its Facebook page. On Wednesday evening, visitors to the news site were greeted by an error message. Konfront added that PM Péter Magyar is erasing the past with this move. On Wednesday evening, visitors to the Mandiner website were greeted by an error message; none of the news site’s articles could be accessed. Mandiner.hu website unavailable on September 9, 2026. Photo: Hungary Today On Friday, Finance Minister András Kármán ordered the dismissal of the CEO of the company that publishes Mandiner , who also served as the newspaper’s editor-in-chief. As part of this decision, funding for the newspaper was also cut off effective immediately. Péter Magyar responded to the events, saying that Mandiner had been “lying for years” and that the site had not been updated since the “public funding tap” was turned off. According to former employees of the publication, the government never even opened the “public funding tap” in the first place, and they also explained why no new content had been posted on the site. Three former staff members have launched their own publication called Konfront , which currently has a Facebook page. In their first post, they also took issue with the prime minister’s claims. According to them, Magyar “is not telling the truth,” a statement they later qualified by saying he is “at the very least being misleading.” According to Konfront, Magyar and his team are erasing the past. “The moment when we are at a loss for words”—in another post on Wednesday, they commented on the fact that Mandiner ’s website is no longer accessible. Péter Magyar and his team were not content with simply nationalizing and then shutting down Mandiner : they decided to erase the past!” they wrote, confirming that Mandiner ’s website was inaccessible. “Every article, opinion piece, and interview we have produced over the past few years is gone. The right-wing press in Hungary has suffered yet another cowardly and despicable attack,” the post concluded. Mandiner , published by Mandiner Novum Nonprofit Zrt., became the property of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC) in 2025. As Hungary Today reported, the newspaper ceased publication in print at the end of July. After the government decided to liquidate public-interest asset management foundations (KEKVA) that perform public functions, the Hungarian State took over the responsibilities of the foundation operating the MCC. This took effect on August 31. Update: The mandiner.hu website is once again accessible , but a message greets visitors at the top of the page. Mandiner.hu website accessible again on September 10, 2026, with previously published content available in an archive. Photo: Hungary Today We would like to inform our readers that Mandiner has ceased providing new content; only previously published archival content is available there,” the message at the top of the website states. Related article One of the Last Remaining Conservative Media Ends Print Production The print edition of Mandiner is ceasing publication after nearly seven years.
